items.title: Preschool math blasts off in Mississippi
items.summary:
CORINTH, Miss. — Vaughn Dodd is using Magna-Tiles to make a rocketship, carefully selecting different shapes for the nose cone and the tail. The four-year-old pre-K student at Corinth Elementary School knows that a diamond shape is called a rhombus. She knows the sun is a circle. 

Proficiency with translucent plastic shapes may not lead directly to a future job in Mississippi’s growing aerospace industry, but it’s not a bad launching pad for any number of careers that involve mathematical concepts.

Vaughn’s teacher, Kayla Wood, leads a range of activities in the name of math, some with the whole class and some in small groups. Toys like the Magna-Tiles, which support counting, sorting and other skills, are available for independent play. 

“There are no worksheets here,” Wood said. “We don’t do worksheets at any time, even during literacy. We can form letters and numbers with Play-Doh. It’s very hands-on.”

Wood is implementing Building Blocks, the math component of the Mississippi Beginnings curriculum for state-funded pre-K programs. Mississippi is the first state to mandate a math curriculum for its preschool program, which currently serves around 8,700 children, or a quarter of the state’s population of four-year-olds. The rollout of the program started in 2022 and is expected to be in all state-funded preschools by August 2027.

Kayla Wood and her students during a morning of learning at Kossuth Elementary. Starting in the 2027-28 school year, every state-funded pre-K program in Mississippi will be required to use a common early childhood math curriculum called…
items.t: Preschool math blasts off in Mississippi

items.title: Students want hands-on training in the work of democracy. Colleges are answering
items.summary:
KENOSHA, Wis. — Andrew Staff knew the data. The sophomore at the University of Wisconsin-Madison had helped create an information packet for the 26 residents of Kenosha County, each randomly selected and paid $100 to spend a Saturday confronting the local housing crunch. The key question: Could factory-built dwellings help? 

But by the end of the six-hour session, during which residents raised and wrestled with one another’s concerns, Staff’s head was spinning. Affordability was just one factor, he noted, ticking off others such as proximity to parks and transportation and the fact that not every resident actually wants their own house. 

Days later, Staff switched his major from political science to public policy, newly offered this fall at the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s La Follette School of Public Affairs, which had helped organize the Kenosha event in part to give students real-world experience. 

UW-Madison sophomore Andrew Staff, who helped prepare background materials for housing assembly, talks with participants during the session. Darren Hauck for The Hechinger Report 

“I don’t just want to think about political theory,” said Staff. “I want to get out there and do things.” 

It’s no secret that Gen Z is unhappy with the direction of the country , distrustful of government and concerned about political polarization. But there’s also evidence they want to do something about it: Seventy-nine percent of those polled in April 2026 felt they could make a difference by voting and participating in the democratic process; 38 percent want to run for state or local…
items.t: Students want hands-on training in the work of democracy. Colleges are answering

items.title: States step up their role picking winners among college majors and training programs
items.summary:
For years, higher education policy has focused on getting more Americans into college and helping more of them graduate. Now the emphasis has shifted to another question: What are students and the general public getting out of these degrees?

Colleges are being pressed to show that their graduates find good jobs and earn enough to justify the cost of their education. And as criticism of higher education mounts, colleges face additional pressure to show that they are fueling their regional economies.

State policymakers are responding. Both red and blue states are stepping up their efforts to identify which fields are most needed for producing future workers and using those lists to steer subsidies to academic programs — everything from short-term training to graduate school. 

A new 50-state report released today by HCM Strategists, a firm that advises on and advocates for higher education policies, documents how states are identifying high-priority fields of study. It’s something of a central planning exercise, trying to predict what will be needed in the future. Some states rely on labor-market data, including wages and projections of occupational growth. Others use human judgment and advice from employers and industry experts. Still others combine the two.

The stakes are high. Roughly half the states incorporate their priority lists into funding formulas, giving colleges additional money for producing degrees in designated fields. Thirty-five states help pay for the costs of starting up a new degree program in high-priority fields.

items.t: States step up their role picking winners among college majors and training programs

items.title: How a class on climate change leaves students feeling ‘energized’
items.summary:
Jeffrey Seidman holds a doctorate in philosophy. He spent much of his first two decades as a college professor helping students interpret texts by writers like Aristotle, Plato and Kant. And yet Seidman, of Vassar College, also teaches one of the most compelling classes on climate change I’ve come across.

The course, Climate Solutions and Climate Careers: Finding Your Place in the Climate Fight , teaches students about the technologies, policies and strategies behind the clean energy transition, and how to advance them. It’s built on the idea that virtually every career — in fields as diverse as law, finance, education and urban planning — can play a role in combating the climate crisis. 

Students spend two classes per week studying solutions, such as electrifying transportation, greening the grid and bringing clean energy to the developing world. On Fridays, they hear from an outside speaker whose career is devoted to advancing climate solutions. Past speakers have included Emma Fisher, co-founder of Climate Cabinet, which backs candidates for local and state office who are supportive of climate action, and Zoe Samuel, a venture partner at Starshot Capital, which invests in climate technology like ultra-efficient heat pumps and food additives to reduce livestock methane emissions. Seidman also runs a website to bring lessons from his class to a wider audience.

items.title: Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students | Ebony Riddell Bamber
items.summary:
In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem

In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage.

When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan.

Ebony Riddell Bamber is the programme director of the Scott Trust’s Legacies of Enslavement programme

Election officials will recount all of the ballots cast for and against a $73 million tax increase to benefit Jeffco Public Schools after a final tally showed the measure passing by just 327 votes.

“Every vote matters, and when an election comes down to a handful of votes, we want voters to have complete confidence in the outcome,” Jefferson County Clerk and Recorder Amanda Gonzalez said in a statement Friday announcing the recount.

Under state law, a recount is triggered if the margin between passing and failing is one half of one percent or less. Gonzalez said the recount will start Nov. 24 and be completed by Dec. 4.

There’s a lot at stake for Jeffco Public Schools, which is under financial pressure due to declining enrollment. District leaders have said Jeffco, Colorado’s second largest district with 74,000 students, needs the money to stave off further budget cuts.

New York City public schools not only met the state-mandated targets to shrink classes, they surpassed the goal, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Friday.

Nearly three-quarters of classes across New York City’s public schools are capped at 20 to 25 students, depending on the grade.

The city cleared the state’s benchmark for two reasons. First, state lawmakers moved the goal post when they agreed in June to give the city more time to comply with the law, requiring 70% of classes meet the caps this school year instead of the original target of 80%.

Additionally, the city made a change in which classes it counted toward class-size compliance. Officials added to the calculation for the first time “cluster” classes in elementary schools — courses like science, art, physical education, and music that are not taught by students’ typical classroom teacher. Most AI tools don’t help students learn. Education-specific AI tools aren’t necessarily better than general purpose chatbots. And even tools that help teachers save time can have unintended consequences for students.

Those are the conclusions from a review of 52 studies on the use of artificial intelligence in educational settings released Tuesday by the AI Hub for Education, part of Stanford University’s SCALE Initiative, which studies which classroom interventions and tools actually work.

The authors of the report aren’t throwing in the towel on AI in education. There is still very little research on AI in K-12 settings in the United States — many of the studies come from other countries or involve college students — and the technology has potential to provide personalized assistance for students and remove some of the tedium from teachers’ jobs.

That potential is worth developing, said Susanna Loeb, faculty director at the SCALE Initiative and an author of the report.

items.title: With free-tuition promises, some colleges try to untangle confusion over what they cost
items.summary:
MIDDLEBURY, Vt. — Stately buildings of Vermont limestone surround meticulously tended lawns at the edge of a New England village that looks like it’s the setting for a Hallmark Christmas movie.

There’s a golf course on this campus. The student-faculty ratio is an exclusive 9-to-1. And an undergraduate tour guide is telling visiting prospective applicants about a classmate who spent a semester learning how to forage in Malaysia. 

Middlebury College looks and sounds … expensive. But like other universities and colleges, it’s working hard to persuade people that it’s not.

Middlebury has announced that, starting next year, students from families with annual household incomes up to $175,000 can enroll tuition-free . It becomes the latest of a growing number of schools to make this kind of promise, including Princeton (for most families earning up to $250,000, with typical assets), the University of Chicago ($250,000), MIT ($200,000), Harvard ($200,000), Swarthmore ($200,000) and Davidson ($175,000).

These may seem like generous expansions of financial aid; after all, $175,000 is more than double the nation’s median household income . But while it’s true that few additional families will benefit — 35 to 50 in the incoming class at Middlebury, which typically enrolls about 630 new students per year, the college says — most people in those earnings categories already attend without having to pay tuition.

items.t: With free-tuition promises, some colleges try to untangle confusion over what they cost

items.title: Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve | Simon Jenkins
items.summary:
For all the supposed improvements, inspectors still obsess over statistics and adjectives, but surely school success depends on teachers and parents

The government regulation of state schools by Ofsted in England is a fiasco. Following the 2023 suicide of the Reading headteacher Ruth Perry, after her school was downgraded from outstanding to inadequate, Ofsted appears to have referred to a dictionary. Single words were replaced by colour-coded report cards, which use a wider range of different adjectives to grade abstractions such as personal development and wellbeing, achievement and leadership. Never has the concept of “education” seemed so empty.

The reaction of the teaching profession to the new code has itself been devastating, as highlighted in a recent survey that showed more than half of headteachers in England polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are now considering early retirement as a result of the experience. This sense of misery was also illustrated in a poll conducted by the National Education Union one year on from the introduction of the new framework, with 65% saying it is the same as or worse than before.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

items.title: In split vote, Denver school board approves closure of Robert F. Smith STEAM Academy
items.summary:
Did you know search engines like Google are changing the way you see news? Keep Chalkbeat’s valuable education coverage at the top of your feeds by clicking here and checking the box next to our name.

Robert F. Smith STEAM Academy will close at the end of the school year after the Denver school board voted 4-2 Thursday to shutter it. The high school, which was modeled on historically Black colleges and universities, has just 24 students this year.

Board Vice President Monica Hunter and member John Youngquist voted no. Hunter, a former Denver teacher who works for the statewide teachers union, asked about pausing the vote until an agreement granting concessions to teachers at the school could be finalized.

Superintendent Alex Marrero said the school district was done negotiating. He said the two sides verbally agreed on a $1,000 payment to the teachers, plus protections for international teachers with work visas. Marrero said the district rejected other requests. Hunter said those included giving non-tenured teachers two paid days off to interview for other jobs.

“The rationale is this is precedent setting,” Marrero said, “and potentially we have some more (school) consolidations coming, and it would not behoove us to honor those indefinitely.”
items.t: In split vote, Denver school board approves closure of Robert F. Smith STEAM Academy
